Read top to bottom. Every card, label and arrow is editable. Blue = current facts; green = keep / proposed direction; yellow = assumption / trade-off; red = risk.
Your reference layout, adapted to CAPY. Non-functional requirements describe quality and capacity, not excluded features.
FUNCTIONAL / what the customer can do
Find available slots; book; look up upcoming appointments; confirm, cancel and
Ask about services and prices. Receive text and voice through Telegram. Reply
Multiple businesses: each customer, catalog, schedule and booking must stay in
Current gaps: voice replies are not implemented; FAQ answers use catalog fields
and fixed templates, not a general knowledge base.
100k monthly ACTIVE users across businesses. This is not 100k concurrent
p95 text reply <= 5 seconds: webhook receipt to Telegram accepting the reply.
Voice must be benchmarked by recording duration.
99.9% daily availability: time-based equivalent is 86.4 seconds unavailable per
day. A monthly window is different.
Track failed scheduling journeys, not just HTTP 200 acknowledgments. An error
reply is not a successful booking.
02 Capacity: why 11 workers is only an example
Start with demand and processing time. Monthly users alone cannot determine replica count.
100,000 users x 3 conversations x 8 incoming turns
Planning assumptions; replace with observed traffic.
Daily peaks can be much higher than the average.
Neither is a measured production requirement.
Little's Law: L = arrival rate x mean time
Processing-only time counts active work. Total elapsed
70% is a planning target for concurrency, not necessarily
Requires 8-way concurrency and 3s service time to be
Audio duration, tokens and GPU capacity drive inference
A cafe receiving 2 customers/minute, each staying 10 minutes, has about 20 customers inside on average. CAPY is the same queueing idea. Averages do not describe
bursts or p95 latency. Keep warm spare capacity; autoscaling reacts after demand changes.
03 Architecture: current implementation vs proposed scaling
Keep one application codebase. Separate process roles only where they need different concurrency, resources or failure handling.

sequentially. Audio, model calls and delivery

Arrows show the main work path. PostgreSQL is ONE database; Python domain services run inside workers.
Senders return replies to Telegram. Audio preparation and reminders use separate bounded work pools.
04 Sequence: booking, retries and the crash window
A durable inbox prevents lost accepted messages. Idempotent writes prevent repeated business effects. Neither guarantees exactly-once Telegram delivery.
Current: recover_interrupted() sends a check-your-appointments message instead
of replaying the graph. Safe, but less convenient.
Proposed: save an immutable command; commit its outcome with the booking;
reconstruct the reply from that outcome. Never reinterpret a possibly committed
WHY THE SAME USER MUST BE SERIALIZED
Message A: show tomorrow's slots. Message B: choose option 1. If B runs before
A finishes, it may read an old offer.
Serialize by business + bot + user. Preserve order for one conversation, not
globally for the entire bot. Handle late arrivals explicitly; per-user locking
05 Database relationships: read the business model first
15 application tables after migrations 0001-0003; excludes Alembic version metadata. PK = primary key; FK = foreign key; 1:N = one-to-many.
One professional can offer several services. One service can be offered by
several professionals. professional_services models this many-to-many
relationship without copying names or prices.
Professionals also have 1:N weekly_availability_rules and 1:N blocked_periods:
recurring opening hours and dated exceptions are different concepts.
Each booking references one business, service, professional and customer.
*Each identity links to 0..1 customer. The unique index permits at most one
identity per business + bot + customer; a customer can link across bots.
reminder_inbox is a demo sink. idempotency_records.resource_id is a logical
booking link, NOT a declared FK.

07 Do we need all these tables?
My assessment: mostly sensible normalization, with a few removable pieces. Table count is not a useful proxy for operational complexity.
Businesses, professionals, services, assignments, weekly hours,
blocks, customers, bookings model separate facts.
Merge only if the product permanently drops that concept.
Update deduplication protects transport; command idempotency protects
business mutations. They have different keys and lifecycles.
Do not remove one just because both mention duplicates.
Makes channel ownership independent of customer contact information.
Merging saves one table only if one bot/account per
customer is a permanent constraint and legacy links are
Only schema references found; currently no working audit feature.
Check real data and external consumers. Use a new forward
Production delivery needs a transport outbox, not a fake inbox.
Migrate CLI/tests and delivery. May replace one table with
Webhook ingestion does not need a long-poll cursor.
After webhook cutover and rollback window.
Do not split every concept into a
One repository with API/worker/sender roles is enough initially.
Split further for measured resource or ownership needs.
Removing unused audit_events and, after webhook cutover, polling offsets takes 15 tables to 13. Replacing reminder_inbox with a real outbox keeps the count at 13. New
durable leases, commands or tenant configuration may add tables again. Optimize responsibilities and correctness, not an arbitrary table target.
08 Static code review: problems and evidence
These are source-level findings. Performance risks are not benchmark results; a database constraint gap is not proof of an exploitable customer endpoint.
HIGH / before horizontal workers / One worker per bot + sequential
Adding replicas fails the bot lock; slow audio/model work delays everyone.
Split roles and serialize only per conversation.
HIGH / before concurrent delivery / Global reply head-of-line
The oldest reply across the bot blocks newer replies, including other chats.
Use per-chat ordering plus safe sender claims.
HIGH / integrity hardening / Tenant consistency is not enforced by
A booking can reference business A and a customer from B at the schema level.
Add composite tenant FKs after cleaning data; retain application ownership
HIGH / before concurrent recovery / Recovery and checkpoints
Recovery sweeps every processing update for the bot. Redis read-modify-write is
not fenced. Add per-conversation leases, expiry and stale-owner rejection.
MEDIUM / measure hot tenants / Business-wide write lock
All booking writes for one business serialize. Deliberate MVP trade-off;
measure lock wait before narrowing locks. Keep exclusion constraints.
MEDIUM / database efficiency / Connection churn and
New DB connections per operation; approximately 3 + 3P queries inside
scheduling_data for P professionals. Add bounded pooling; batch queries if
MEDIUM / retention semantics / delete_thread removes only latest
Earlier checkpoint/write keys and other namespaces remain until TTL. Fine for
eventual expiry, insufficient if full immediate deletion is promised.
MEDIUM / deploy safety / Migrations and demo seeding on API
Fine for local Compose. Do not copy unchanged into multiple production
replicas; use a one-time release migration job.
09 Why constraints matter: prevent invalid state at the boundary
Application authorization answers who may act. Database constraints answer what rows are valid. You need both.
Business A owns booking X. Customer C belongs to business B.
Independent FKs accept A and C because each exists. They do not check that C
Application create/ownership paths do check business/customer identity. The gap
matters for bugs, imports and future writers.
Proposed: UNIQUE(id, business_id) on parents and FOREIGN KEY(customer_id,
business_id) referencing customers(id, business_id). Extend the pattern to
Two users can both see 10:00 as free. Search is only a snapshot. Revalidate
when booking and keep the exclusion constraint as the final race-safe guard.
The occupied interval includes preparation/cleanup buffers. Adjacent half-open
A retry with the same operation key should reuse the committed result. Today
replay reads the current booking row, so it is not an immutable copy of the
10 Autoscaling and failures: what changes the replica count?
More workers help only when the downstream database and model servers have spare capacity.
At least 2 warm replicas; request concurrency + latency
Acknowledge only committed inbox rows. DB failure must not produce a false
Runnable conversations + arrival rate x service time
Do not count 100 queued turns for one user as 100 parallel tasks. Drain
Queue time, tokens/sec, latency, device memory
More application pods cannot fix saturated inference. Warm redundancy is
Isolate expensive audio. Complete transcript before actions. TTS failure
Honor 429 retry_after. More senders cannot raise Telegram limits.
Connections, lock wait, query time; checkpoint bytes
HA/failover plus restore tests. Redis loss means rebuild a draft, never
Start with the existing PostgreSQL ledger as the durable queue. No Kafka, database sharding, separate booking microservice, vector database or multi-region writes
solely because there are 100k monthly users. Add a broker when queue load, fan-out or operational needs justify it. Gemma and Laya are required here; optimize and
benchmark their boundary rather than silently removing one.
The board proposes changes; it does not modify application behavior or remove database tables.
1. Measure traffic, model latency, DB queries/locks and per-bot delivery.
2. Harden tenant constraints and retry tests.
3. Add durable webhook ingestion and per-conversation ownership.
4. Separate senders; remove global reply blocking.
5. Add bounded concurrency, pooling and safe crash recovery.
6. Implement real reminders, TTS and approved FAQ content.
8. Remove obsolete tables only with data/consumer checks and forward
Why can a webhook return 200 before the customer gets a reply?
Why do updates and commands need different idempotency keys?
Why is 100k MAU insufficient to size workers?
Why is Redis not the source of booking truth?
Why can one delayed reply block unrelated users today?
Why do separate FKs not guarantee the same tenant?
Which table would you remove first, and what would you check?
What happens if a worker dies just after the booking commits?
